hints: Start from the colour of the starting complex, $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$, and think about what you normally see when a transition metal aqua ion meets $\text{OH}^-$ ions.
Think about how many $\text{OH}^-$ ions are needed to neutralise the 2+ charge and what happens to the six water ligands when the neutral hydroxide forms.
Decide whether any ligand has replaced water in the coordination sphere or whether a solid has simply come out of solution, then link this to precipitation versus ligand exchange.
walkthrough:
Picture the starting solution**
You have $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ in solution, which is the familiar pale blue copper(II) solution. When you add aqueous sodium hydroxide you are adding a good source of $\text{OH}^-$ ions. Hydroxide is a base and will react with the acidic aqua complex.

Form the neutral hydroxide solid**
Two $\text{OH}^-$ ions balance the 2+ charge. They pull the $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ out of solution as neutral copper(II) hydroxide, $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$, which cannot stay dissolved. That is why you see a blue solid or blue precipitate, even in excess $\text{NaOH}$ because $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$ does not redissolve.

Write the balanced ionic equation**
Keep the copper complex together on the left and release all six waters:
$$\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu(OH)}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Check atoms and charge: one Cu, eight O, fourteen H on each side, and zero net charge on each side.

Classify the reaction correctly**
No ammonia or other ligand has entered the coordination sphere to give a new soluble complex. A solid has formed from ions in solution, driven by acid-base neutralisation of the aqua complex. So call it precipitation, which here is also an acid-base reaction.

Final answer: Observation: blue solid / blue precipitate.
Equation: $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu(OH)}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
Type of reaction: precipitation / acid-base

hints: Recall the two stage observation with $\text{NH}_3$(aq): a blue precipitate first forms, then think about what excess ammonia does to that precipitate.
Focus on $\text{NH}_3$ as a ligand that can replace water, and recall how many $\text{NH}_3$ molecules fit around $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in the final complex.
Consider whether the coordination number changes and whether a solid or a new soluble complex is the final product, to name the reaction type.
walkthrough:
Follow the colour story in excess**
With a little aqueous ammonia you first get the same pale blue $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$ precipitate, because $\text{NH}_3$ in water provides $\text{OH}^-$. In excess ammonia that precipitate dissolves. The end point you must report is a clear, intense dark blue or deep blue solution, not a solid.

See ammonia as a competing ligand**
$\text{NH}_3$ can donate its lone pair to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and swap places with water. Copper(II) favours four $\text{NH}_3$ ligands in the plane, leaving two waters still attached. That gives the complex ion $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$, which has the strong dark blue colour.

Write the exchange equation**
Show four $\text{NH}_3$ molecules replacing four waters, with four waters released:
$$\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Charge stays 2+ on both sides and ligands balance: six waters on the left, two plus four on the right.

Name the reaction type**
Water ligands have been directly swapped for ammonia ligands with no change in oxidation state and no solid remaining. That is the classic definition of ligand exchange, also accepted as ligand substitution, displacement or replacement.

Final answer: Observation: dark blue / deep blue solution.
Equation: $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$
Type of reaction: ligand exchange / substitution / displacement

hints: Use the clues: a blue solution means $\text{Cu}^{2+}$(aq) is present, and a red-brown solid points to a familiar elemental metal, then work back to the $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ starting oxidation state of +1.
Think about what it means when the same element (+1) ends up both higher (+2) and lower (0), and what name is given to that special type of redox.
walkthrough:
Decode the two products from colour**
The oxide here is copper(I) oxide, $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$. Hot dilute sulfuric acid gives a blue solution, which is the signature of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$(aq), so X is $\text{CuSO}_4$ in solution. The red-brown solid is the characteristic colour of elemental copper metal, so Y is $\text{Cu}$.

Spot the oxidation state split**
In $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ copper is +1. In the products it is +2 in $\text{CuSO}_4$ and 0 in $\text{Cu}$. The same species has been simultaneously oxidised (+1 to +2) and reduced (+1 to 0). When one oxidation state splits both ways like this, call it disproportionation, which is a special type of redox reaction.

Final answer: X: $\text{CuSO}_4$ / copper(II) sulfate
Y: $\text{Cu}$ / copper
type of reaction: redox / disproportionation
